entry.title: on meaning
entry.content:
I've been meaning to write this blog post for a while now, constantly analysing draft after draft, trying to make my scattered consciousness coherent. As I near the one year anniversary of my first (and only) blog post titled 'on life', the realisation that life truly waits for none is becoming more apparent to me. And in this state of mind, I question who I'm willing to become before I die?

I live in a world of potentialities, rather than a world of commitments. I talk of great adventures I'll embark on, but I freeze once confronted with concrete plans. I'm the quintessential puer aeternus, the eternal manchild archetype described by Carl Jung whose influence can only be subdued by the drab and dreary work that paves the road to the achievement of a higher goal.

And it is precisely this drab and dreary work that I'm most afraid of. But it hasn't always been this way. I do remember the countless hours I poured into my academic pursuits, sometimes at the expense of fun and relaxation. That flame is still flickering within the deepest recesses of my soul, and I dream of rekindling the inferno that it once was.

I've been re-reading 'Man's Search For Meaning' by Viktor Frankl in hopes of inspiring a personal revival of sorts. And the following passage is one I'll continue to read for the rest of my life:

It is a peculiarity of man that he can only live by looking to the future - sub specie aeternitatis. And this is his salvation in the most difficult moments of his existence, although he sometimes has to force his mind to the task.

— Viktor Frankl

Frankl was able to find meaning in his truly unexplainable suffering as a victim of the holocaust by looking solely into the future. He hoped to complete his scientific paper, reunite with his wife and experience life outside the barbed wire confines of his camp. It was in this that his suffering had meaning. And it's from his experience that I must ask myself the following question: What does the future ask of me?

And this is something I'm certain I won't be able to answer on a train ride to Liverpool. I'll have to ponder and seriously spend quality time formulating a potential image of the future; one with which my apparent meaningless suffering takes meaning.

entry.title: on life
entry.content:
Life is short. You probably already know that. But how should we spend our limited time on this planet? What pursuits should we undertake? Who do we strive to become?

I've always been in a constant state of existential panic, as someone who, from a very young age, spent countless hours pondering the meaning and purpose of existence. Nothing my parents and culture could every teach me could satisfy the salient questions on my mind.

I write this because for the very first time in my life, I don't really have a clue on what do next. Recently starting a 9-5, a weird sense of finality is brewing within me. Is this it? Is working for the rest of my life really my destiny?

I plan on reading Tuesdays with Morrie this week. Hopefully I end up finding the answer?
